Series::kron¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::kron(const Series& other) const -> Series

What It Does¶

kron() is the Kronecker product. For two matrices A ([m, n]) and B ([p, q]) it produces the [m*p, n*q] block matrix

       | A[0,0]*B   A[0,1]*B   ...  |
A ⊗ B = | A[1,0]*B   A[1,1]*B   ...  |
       |   ...                      |

— every entry of A scaled by the whole of B, tiled into place. It shows up in tensor-product constructions: building a 2-D operator from two 1-D ones, expanding a state space, forming separable filters.

kron() is computed as a broadcast multiply of reshaped operands (A reshaped to [m, 1, n, 1] times B reshaped to [1, p, 1, q], folded back to [m*p, n*q]), so it is a plain differentiable expression — no special backward.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&)

The right operand B. For the 2-D form both operands are matrices; other ranks fall back to the outer product of the flattened operands reshaped to the concatenation of the two input shapes.

For non-matrix inputs, read that rule literally. If A has shape [a0,a1] and B has shape [b0], the result shape is [a0,a1,b0]; values are ordered as every flattened value of A multiplying every flattened value of B. This differs from the block folding used by the dedicated matrix case.

Returns¶

Series The [m*p, n*q] Kronecker product (2-D form).

Gradient¶

kron() is differentiable in both operands. It is bilinear, so the backward is the matching contraction of the upstream gradient with the other operand.

Examples¶

Example 1. A 2 x 2 Kronecker product.

auto a = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto b = pluss::make_series({{0.0, 5.0}, {6.0, 7.0}});

std::cout << a.kron(b);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[4,4], strides=[4,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=16, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 5, 0, 10],
  [6, 7, 12, 14],
  [0, 15, 0, 20],
  [18, 21, 24, 28]]

The top-left 2 x 2 block is 1 * b, the top-right is 2 * b, and so on.

Example 2. The gradient with respect to A: each A[i,j] sees the whole of B.

auto a = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto b = pluss::make_series({{0.0, 5.0}, {6.0, 7.0}});
a.tracks_slope_(true);

a.kron(b).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dL/da=" << a.sensitivity();

Output¶

dL/da=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[18, 18],
  [18, 18]]

With g = ones, every dL/dA[i,j] = sum(B) = 0 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 18.

Example 3. Vector inputs use the general concatenated-shape rule.

auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0});
std::cout << a.kron(b);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[10, 20, 30],
  [20, 40, 60]]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The 2-D form is the well-defined case: [m,n] ⊗ [p,q] -> [m*p, n*q].

  • Integer inputs are promoted to floating point.

  • The result grows multiplicatively — [100, 100] ⊗ [100, 100] is a 10000 x 10000 matrix.

Summary¶

kron(other) is the Kronecker (tensor) product:

  • [m,n] ⊗ [p,q] -> [m*p, n*q], each A[i,j] scaling a full copy of B

  • a differentiable broadcast-multiply expression

  • promotes integer input to floating point

See Also¶

  • Series::outer: the vector special case ([m] ⊗ [n], up to a reshape).

  • SeriesLinearAlgAccessor::matmul: the ordinary matrix product.

  • Series::repeat: plain tiling without the per-block scaling.
